headings.title: Introduction to Dietary Assessment in Nursing
headings.content: Dietary assessment is a systematic method of collecting and evaluating an individual's food and nutrient intake to determine their nutritional status. In Nigerian clinical practice, nurses often serve as the first point of contact for identifying patients at risk of malnutrition, making foundational knowledge of dietary intake essential. This evaluation helps uncover subtle nutrient deficiencies or excesses before physical clinical signs manifest. By understanding what a patient eats at home or in the community, the healthcare team can align medical interventions with local dietary habits and food availability.

headings.title: Purposes and Objectives of Dietary Intake Evaluation
headings.content:
Assessing food intake serves multiple clinical and public health objectives. 
- **Screening**: Identifying individuals who are malnourished or at high risk of developing nutritional deficiencies.
- **Monitoring**: Tracking the effectiveness of a prescribed therapeutic diet over time.
- **Epidemiology**: Studying the relationship between specific food patterns and chronic diseases within the Nigerian population.
- **Education**: Providing a baseline to educate patients on making healthier local food choices.

headings.title: Retrospective Dietary Assessment Methods
headings.content:
Retrospective methods require the patient to look backward and recall what they ate in the past. These tools are commonly used because they impose minimal burden on the patient's daily routine.

- **24-Hour Dietary Recall**: The patient reports all foods and beverages consumed during the past 24 hours or the previous day, often using visual aids like food models or local household measures like standard plates and cups.
- **Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ)**: A structured checklist asking how often, on average, a person consumed specific food items over a designated period such as a month or year.

While convenient, these methods rely heavily on the patient's memory and can be skewed by intentional under-reporting of unhealthy foods.

headings.title: Prospective Dietary Assessment Methods
headings.content:
Prospective methods capture dietary intake as it happens, reducing the errors associated with memory recall. 

| Method | Description | Clinical Utility |
|---|---|---|
| **Food Diary / Record** | Patient writes down all food and drink at the time of consumption over 3 to 7 days. | Highly accurate for motivated individuals, but requires literacy. |
| **Weighed Food Record** | Patient or caregiver weighs every food item using a scale before eating and weighs leftovers. | Gold standard for research, but high burden and impractical in busy wards. |

In busy Nigerian healthcare settings, prospective records are often challenging due to patient literacy levels, time constraints, and the communal nature of eating from a shared bowl.

headings.title: Evaluating Nutritional Adequacy Using Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs)
headings.content:
Once dietary data is gathered, nurses and dietitians compare the reported nutrient intake against established standards known as **Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs)**. These reference values help determine if a patient receives enough energy, vitamins, and minerals. 

- **Estimated Average Requirement (EAR)**: Intake level estimated to meet the nutrient needs of half the healthy individuals in a life stage and gender group.
- **Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)**: Average daily dietary intake level sufficient to meet the nutrient requirement of nearly all healthy individuals.
- **Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL)**: Maximum daily intake level likely to pose no adverse health effects.

headings.title: Challenges, Biases, and Limitations in Dietary Reporting
headings.content: Obtaining accurate dietary data is notoriously difficult. Patients frequently alter their reporting due to social desirability bias, intentionally under-reporting foods perceived as unhealthy (like fried foods or sugary drinks) and over-reporting healthy options like vegetables. Memory lapses, inaccurate portion size estimation, and the challenge of measuring mixed Nigerian dishes like pot-cooked jollof rice or egusi soup add significant error. Nurses must interpret dietary data cautiously, triangulating findings with anthropometric measurements and biochemical blood tests rather than relying on food logs alone.

headings.title: Integrating Dietary Assessment into the Nursing Process and Care Plans
headings.content: Dietary assessment findings must be actively woven into the nursing process. During the assessment phase, the nurse collects food history alongside vital signs. In the diagnosis phase, data supports labels like *Imbalanced Nutrition: Less Than Body Requirements*. Planning and implementation involve collaborating with clinical dietitians and family members to design culturally appropriate meal plans utilizing affordable local foods. Finally, evaluation involves monitoring weight changes and clinical labs to see if the nutritional interventions succeeded.
